faq.a: Malaria can cause chronic bone‑marrow suppression and splenic sequestration; repeat testing ensures parasites are cleared and looks for co‑existing causes.
faq.q: Why does anaemia persist after treating malaria?

faq.a: When ferritin exceeds 1000 µg/L or there is evidence of cardiac or hepatic iron deposition in a transfusion‑dependent patient.
faq.q: When should iron chelation be started?

faq.a: Usually not, because transfusions already supply iron; additional oral iron risks overload.
faq.q: Can oral iron be given if the patient is already receiving transfusions?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with known TB on treatment remains anaemic (Hb 7 g/dL) after 6 weeks – what is your next diagnostic step? — Check reticulocyte count and peripheral smear to differentiate marrow failure from ongoing blood loss.
How does chronic malaria cause refractory anaemia and what additional test helps? — Malaria suppresses erythropoiesis; a repeat thick film and PCR for low‑grade parasitaemia clarify persistence.

A patient with β‑thalassaemia intermedia presents with worsening fatigue; ferritin is 1500 µg/L. What complication are you most concerned about and how to monitor? — Cardiac iron overload; obtain ECG and echocardiography, consider T2* MRI if available.
Why is erythropoiesis‑stimulating therapy avoided in untreated HIV infection? — It may worsen uncontrolled viral replication and increase thrombotic risk.

A pregnant woman with hookworm infection has persistent anaemia despite iron tablets. What is the next management step? — Give a single dose of albendazole (after first trimester) and repeat stool exam.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with refractory anaemia mandates urgent referral? — New chest pain or syncope suggesting myocardial ischaemia.

How would you differentiate iron‑deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease when ferritin is 150 µg/L? — Measure transferrin saturation; <20 % suggests iron deficiency, >20 % points to chronic disease.

In a resource‑limited setting without bone‑marrow biopsy, how can you suspect a primary marrow failure? — Persistent low retic count (<2 %) with normal iron studies and no evidence of bleeding or infection.
ai.title: Refractory Anaemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Refractory anaemia is anaemia that persists despite appropriate treatment of the identified cause, often due to missed or ongoing pathology or ineffective erythropoiesis. It is common in low‑resource settings where infections, chronic disease and hereditary disorders coexist.

b: Exclude laboratory error (repeat CBC)
Confirm adherence to therapy and correct dosing
Check for ongoing blood loss, hemolysis, or marrow failure
sections.p: Anaemia that does not improve after 4–6 weeks of appropriate therapy for the presumed cause, with haemoglobin remaining at least 2 g/dL below the normal range for age and sex.

b: Mild: Hb 10–11 g/dL, minimal symptoms
Moderate: Hb 8–9.9 g/dL, fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL, tachycardia, orthostasis, chest pain
sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin level, mirroring WHO anaemia classification, and by clinical impact.

b: Chronic infections: malaria, tuberculosis, HIV‑associated opportunistic infections
Chronic inflammation: rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease
Hereditary ineffective erythropoiesis: β‑thalassaemia intermedia, sickle‑cell disease, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia
Gastro‑intestinal blood loss: hookworm, ulcer disease, colorectal cancer
Drug‑induced marrow suppression: antiretrovirals, anti‑TB drugs, chemotherapy
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most frequent causes are infections, chronic disease and hereditary disorders.

b: Pallor of conjunctivae and nail beds
Heart rate >100 bpm at rest
Spleen palpable >2 cm below costal margin in dyserythropoietic states
sections.p: Patients present with persistent fatigue, pallor, tachycardia and, when severe, dyspnoea at rest. In hereditary forms, skeletal deformities or splenomegaly may be evident.

t.a: Full blood count with reticulocyte count
t.b: Is the anaemia regenerative? Low retic (<2 %) suggests marrow failure; high retic (>2 %) suggests peripheral loss or haemolysis
Are there abnormal red cell morphologies (e.g., target cells, schistocytes, multinucleated erythroblasts) that point to specific aetiologies
Is iron deficiency present (low ferritin) or is iron overload developing (ferritin >1000 µg/L) from repeated transfusions
Is chronic kidney disease contributing via reduced erythropoietin
Are chronic viral infections driving inflammation or marrow suppression

t.a: Stool occult blood or helminth ova
t.b: Is there occult gastrointestinal blood loss or hookworm infection
Does the marrow show hypercellularity with erythroid hyperplasia (ineffective erythropoiesis) or aplasia

b: Chest pain or syncope → possible myocardial ischaemia
New onset heart failure signs (edema, JVD)
Serum ferritin >1000 µg/L with cardiac or hepatic dysfunction
sections.p: Unrecognised refractory anaemia can lead to high‑output cardiac failure, severe hypoxia, and iron overload in transfusion‑dependent patients.

b: Infection: appropriate anti‑malarial, anti‑TB, or antiretroviral therapy
Chronic kidney disease: start erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents if affordable
Hereditary dyserythropoiesis: consider regular transfusion with iron chelation (deferasirox) when transfusion‑dependent
Avoid high‑dose vitamin C in iron overload as it increases absorption
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive measures while monitoring for iron overload.

b: Review Hb every 4 weeks until stable
Check ferritin every 3 months in transfused patients
Educate on malaria prophylaxis, deworming, and nutrition rich in iron and folate
sections.p: Regular monitoring of haemoglobin, reticulocyte count and iron status guides therapy adjustments.

b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia unresponsive to oral iron (often due to malabsorption or ongoing loss)
Aplastic anaemia (primary marrow failure, low retic count)
Hemolytic anaemia (high retic, jaundice, LDH elevation)
sections.p: Conditions that cause persistent anaemia despite treatment but have different pathophysiology.

b: Ferritin may be normal or high in inflammation, masking true iron deficiency
Reticulocyte count can be falsely low in acute infection despite marrow activity
Peripheral smear may miss subtle dyserythropoietic changes without expert review
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite serious disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid fall in haemoglobin >2 g/dL in 48 h
